pos: v. (second person singular present of be; rendering Hebrew 'attah hu and the verbless clause, Greek ei)
etymology: From Saxon eart, the second person singular present of beon, to be. It pairs with thou as are pairs with ye. Distinguish it entirely from the noun art, skill or craft, which is a separate word from Latin ars.
biblical_def: Art is the second person singular of the verb to be: thou art, where a plural would require ye are. Because it can only follow thou, it is the verb of every confession and every accusation made to one person. God's first recorded question after the fall uses it: “Where art thou?” (Genesis 3:9) — not an enquiry after information but a summons to account. Peter's confession uses it: “Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God”, and so does Nathanael's: “Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel”. The risen Christ uses it to indict a whole church in the person of its angel: “I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot” (Revelation 3:15). And the psalmist uses it as the ground of all his petitions: “Thou art my King, O God: command deliverances for Jacob” (Psalm 44:4). In every case the word fastens an identity on someone. It is the grammar of what a person actually is before God, as opposed to what he says or does, and Scripture is full of it because God deals with persons and not with abstractions.
webster_summary: The second person singular of the present tense of the verb to be; used only with thou. In Scripture it is the verb of confession and of indictment — thou art the Christ, thou art the man, thou art neither cold nor hot.
webster_full: ART, v. [Sax. eart.] The second person singular of the present tense of the substantive verb; as, thou art.
2. It is used only with the pronoun thou; with ye or you the form is are.
3. In the modern style the distinction is lost, you being used with are for both numbers.
4. ART, n. [L. ars, artis.] Skill in performance; a system of rules for effecting a given end. This is a wholly distinct word.
5. In Scripture, Where art thou? Gen. 3; Thou art the Christ, Matt. 16; thou art neither cold nor hot, Rev. 3.
corruption_summary: The confession thou art the Christ is regularly reduced to a statement of personal preference — what Jesus is to me — rather than a statement of what He is in Himself. The verb will not permit it: art asserts being, not sentiment.
corruption_paragraphs: A widespread habit of speech in modern religion converts every confession into an autobiography. Jesus is said to be my Saviour, my Lord, what He means to me — and none of that is false, but as a substitute for the objective claim it is a serious loss. Peter did not say that Jesus had come to function as the Christ in his experience. He said Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God, and the Lord replied that flesh and blood had not revealed it. The confession is a statement about the person of Christ that would be true if Peter had never made it, and the believer's part is not to constitute it but to see it.

The same verb makes the Laodicean indictment inescapable. Christ does not tell that church what it feels or what it intends; He tells it what it is — thou art neither cold nor hot, and afterward, wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked. The church's own estimate ran the other way, for it said I am rich, and increased with goods. Between the self-assessment and the verdict of Christ there is no negotiation, and self-knowledge for a Christian begins by accepting His sentence rather than his own.
roots_summary: Hebrew often has no copula at all, setting two nouns side by side (the LORD my shepherd), or uses the pronoun hu to bind them; Greek uses ei, the second singular of eimi; Saxon eart gives the English form.
roots_lines: Hebrew verbless clause — the ordinary way of saying thou art, by simple apposition without any verb, as in Psalm 44:4.
Hebrew hu (H1931) — he, that one; used as a copula to join subject and predicate where emphasis is wanted.
Greek ei (G1488) — thou art; the second person singular present of eimi, to be.
Greek eimi (G1510) — I am; the same verb that stands behind the divine name in John 8:58.
Saxon eart — the Old English second singular present, preserved by the Authorized Version alongside thou.
usage: Of God summoning the hiding sinner to account: Where art thou? (Genesis 3:9).
Of confession made to Christ in person: thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel (John 1:49).
Of Christ's verdict on a self-satisfied church: thou art neither cold nor hot (Revelation 3:15).
scriptures: And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?
Nathanael answered and saith unto him, Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel.
I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot.
Thou art my King, O God: command deliverances for Jacob.

pos: v. (second person singular past of be; rendering Hebrew perfect forms, Greek imperfect es)
etymology: The past tense answering to art, as was answers to is. Saxon wære. It is used with thou only, and the Authorized Version keeps it wherever one person's past condition is in view.
biblical_def: Wast is thou wast — what one person formerly was. Scripture uses it chiefly for two purposes, and both are pastoral. The first is the remembrance of bondage as the ground of mercy: “thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in Egypt, and the LORD thy God redeemed thee thence: therefore I command thee to do this thing” (Deuteronomy 24:18). The commandment about the gleanings of the harvest rests on a memory, and Israel is to treat the stranger, the fatherless and the widow as one who has himself been a slave and been bought out. The second is the exposure of what a creature once was before it fell: “Thou wast perfect in thy ways from the day that thou wast created, till iniquity was found in thee” (Ezekiel 28:15). And the first use of all is the LORD's question in Eden — “Who told thee that thou wast naked?” (Genesis 3:11) — where the past tense exposes the newness of shame and traces it to a source. In each case the tense does the work: what a man was governs what he now owes.
webster_summary: The second person singular of the past tense of to be; used only with thou. In Scripture it is the tense of remembered bondage, of shame traced to its source, and of the creature's original estate before iniquity was found in it.
webster_full: WAST, v. The second person singular of the past tense of the substantive verb; as, thou wast.
2. It is used only with thou; with ye or you the form is were.
3. Sax. wære; the same root with was and were, and answering to art in the present.
4. The subjunctive form is wert, used in suppositions and wishes.
5. In Scripture, thou wast a bondman in Egypt, Deut. 24; Thou wast perfect in thy ways, Ezek. 28.
corruption_summary: The command to remember what one was is quietly dropped by the prosperous, and the mercy owed to the stranger goes with it. Israel's obedience was grounded in memory; a people that forgets it was once a bondman becomes hard toward everyone still in bonds.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is the memory of one's own redemption as the motive for mercy. Deuteronomy grounds a whole body of social legislation — gleaning left in the field, wages paid the same day, justice for the fatherless — on the single clause thou wast a bondman in Egypt. The reasoning is not sentimental. A redeemed man who deals hardly with the helpless has forgotten the terms of his own rescue, and the law will not let him forget them.

The New Testament carries the same tense into the gospel. Paul reminds the Corinthians of the catalogue of sins from which some of them came and adds and such were some of you: but ye are washed; the Ephesians are told ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord. The past tense is essential to Christian humility. Where it is lost, the church begins to speak of the world as though its members had never belonged to it, and the tone of its witness hardens into contempt. Where it is kept, the same warnings are given with tears.
roots_summary: Hebrew has no separate past of the copula in most clauses, expressing it by the perfect of hayah or by context; Greek uses es, the imperfect second singular of eimi; Saxon wære gives the English form.
roots_lines: Hebrew hayah (H1961) — to be, to become, to come to pass; its perfect forms supply the past of the copula.
Hebrew 'ebed (H5650) — a servant or bondman; the word behind thou wast a bondman in Egypt.
Greek es (G2258) — thou wast; the imperfect second singular of eimi.
Saxon wære — the Old English past second singular, retained by the Authorized Version with thou.
The tense contrast — wast for the indicative fact, wert for the supposition or the wish.
usage: Of shame traced back to its source: Who told thee that thou wast naked? (Genesis 3:11).
Of remembered bondage as the ground of mercy: thou wast a bondman in Egypt, and the LORD thy God redeemed thee (Deuteronomy 24:18).
Of a creature's original estate before its fall: Thou wast perfect in thy ways from the day that thou wast created (Ezekiel 28:15).
scriptures: And he said, Who told thee that thou wast naked? Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?
But thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in Egypt, and the LORD thy God redeemed thee thence: therefore I command thee to do this thing.
Thou wast perfect in thy ways from the day that thou wast created, till iniquity was found in thee.
What ailed thee, O thou sea, that thou fleddest? thou Jordan, that thou wast driven back?

pos: v. (second person singular past subjunctive of be; rendering Hebrew and Greek conditional constructions)
etymology: The subjunctive counterpart of wast. Where wast states a past fact, wert states a supposition, a condition contrary to fact, or a wish. It occurs only five times in the Authorized Version, and every occurrence is weighty.
biblical_def: Wert is the past subjunctive of be in the second person singular — the mood of the supposed rather than the actual. Its rarity makes each instance memorable. Bildad reasons from a false premise about Job: “If thou wert pure and upright; surely now he would awake for thee” (Job 8:6), a piece of counsel that is grammatically flawless and pastorally wrong, since the LORD Himself had already declared Job perfect and upright. Paul uses it twice for the grafted Gentile: “thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them” (Romans 11:17), and again, “if thou wert cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature, and wert graffed contrary to nature into a good olive tree” (Romans 11:24). The whole argument against Gentile boasting turns on that contrary-to-nature clause: the branch did nothing and could do nothing. And the risen Christ uses it as a wish over Laodicea: “I would thou wert cold or hot” (Revelation 3:15) — a sentence that prefers open opposition to comfortable neutrality.
webster_summary: The second person singular of the past subjunctive of to be; used in suppositions, conditions contrary to fact, and wishes. It occurs five times in the Authorized Version, in Job, the Song, Romans twice, and Revelation.
webster_full: WERT, v. The second person singular of the subjunctive past tense of the substantive verb; as, if thou wert.
2. It differs from wast, which is the indicative and states a fact; wert states a supposition or a wish.
3. It is used only with thou, and belongs wholly to the solemn and scriptural style.
4. Sax. wære; the same root with was, were and wast.
5. In Scripture, If thou wert pure and upright, Job 8; I would thou wert cold or hot, Rev. 3.
corruption_summary: The Laodicean wish — that a lukewarm church were cold rather than tepid — is precisely inverted by a religious culture that prizes moderation and treats decided conviction, in either direction, as the real danger.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ's preference in Revelation 3:15 is startling and is usually softened in the reading. He does not say He would prefer Laodicea hot; He says He would prefer it cold or hot, either one, rather than what it is. Lukewarmness is worse than open coldness because it is unaware of itself and therefore unreachable; the cold man knows he is outside, while the tepid church congratulates itself on balance. A religious atmosphere that treats every strong conviction as extremism and every hesitation as maturity is producing exactly the condition Christ threatens to spue out of His mouth.

The Romans 11 use guards a different error. Paul's grafted branch wert graffed contrary to nature, and the subjunctive keeps the whole action on God's side; a branch is not consulted about its grafting. The apostle draws the conclusion himself — boast not against the branches — and it applies wherever Christians grow proud of a standing they did not create. Bildad's use is the third warning: a supposition offered as diagnosis. If thou wert pure and upright sounds like theology and functions as accusation, and the book of Job exists in part to show what such counsel does to a suffering man.
roots_summary: Neither Hebrew nor Greek has a form answering exactly to wert; the subjunctive force is carried by conditional particles (Hebrew 'im, lu; Greek ei with the indicative or optative), which the translators rendered by the English mood.
roots_lines: Hebrew lu (H3863) — if only, would that; the particle of the wish contrary to fact.
Hebrew 'im (H518) — if; the ordinary conditional particle, as in Bildad's supposition at Job 8:6.
Greek ei (G1487) — if; with the indicative it frames a condition assumed for the sake of argument, as in Romans 11:24.
Greek ophelon (G3785) — would that, I would; the particle of unattainable wish behind Revelation 3:15.
Greek egkentrizo (G1461) — to graft in; the verb governed by wert in both Romans 11 passages.
usage: Of a supposition offered as false comfort: If thou wert pure and upright (Job 8:6).
Of the Gentile branch grafted contrary to nature: thou wert cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature (Romans 11:24).
Of Christ preferring open coldness to lukewarmness: I would thou wert cold or hot (Revelation 3:15).
scriptures: If thou wert pure and upright; surely now he would awake for thee, and make the habitation of thy righteousness prosperous.
And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree;

For if thou wert cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature, and wert graffed contrary to nature into a good olive tree: how much more shall these, which be the natural branches, be graffed into their own olive tree?
I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot.

pos: v. (third person singular present of have; rendering Hebrew perfect forms, Greek echei and the perfect tense)
etymology: From Saxon hæfþ, the third person singular present of habban, to have. It stands where modern English has has. In the Authorized Version it does double duty: possession, and the auxiliary that forms the perfect tense.
biblical_def: Hath is the older has, and in Scripture its most important work is as the auxiliary of the perfect tense — the tense of the finished act whose effect stands. “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” (Acts 10:15): the cleansing is done, and Peter's scruple is therefore out of date. “For the LORD of hosts hath purposed, and who shall disannul it?” (Isaiah 14:27): the purpose is already formed, and the question that follows admits of no answer. The tense is also the instrument of Christ's deepest exposure of the law: “whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart” (Matthew 5:28) — not will commit, not is tempted to commit, but hath committed, the sin complete before any hand has moved. And the serpent's first recorded words misquote a perfect: “God hath said, Ye shall not eat of it” (Genesis 3:3), where the finished speech of God is the very thing under attack. Wherever the Authorized Version writes hath, something is settled.
webster_summary: The third person singular of the present tense of have; the older form of has. In Scripture it is chiefly the auxiliary of the perfect tense — the finished act whose effect remains: God hath cleansed, the LORD hath purposed, he hath committed adultery already in his heart.
webster_full: HATH, v. [Sax. hæfþ.] The third person singular of the present tense of have; contracted in modern usage to has.
2. To possess; to hold as owner; as, he hath riches.
3. As an auxiliary, it forms the perfect tense of other verbs; as, he hath spoken, he hath done.
4. It is retained in the solemn style and throughout the common version of the Scriptures.
5. In Scripture, What God hath cleansed, Acts 10; the LORD of hosts hath purposed, Isa. 14.
corruption_summary: The perfect tense of Scripture is regularly read as a present possibility. What God hath done is turned into what God may do; a finished cleansing becomes an offered one, a settled purpose becomes an intention, and an accomplished sin becomes a temptation not yet yielded to.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrinal cost of blurring the perfect tense is heaviest at the atonement. Scripture speaks of a work finished — it is finished, he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified, what God hath cleansed — and a theology that softens these into offers held out to the willing has changed the gospel's tense. The Reformed doctrine of definite atonement is in large part a refusal to do this: Christ did not make salvation possible, He accomplished it for His people, and the perfect tense in the epistles is the grammatical form of that accomplishment.

Matthew 5:28 shows the same tense used against us, and it is just as commonly softened. The Lord is not describing a man in danger of adultery; He is convicting a man who has already committed it, in the only place where the seventh commandment is finally kept or broken. Popular teaching frequently reduces this to a warning against letting a look go too far, which is precisely the distinction Christ abolishes. The tense is the whole force of the sentence: the sin is complete, the man is guilty, and he needs not better management of his eyes but a new heart.
roots_summary: Hebrew has no verb to have, expressing possession by the preposition le with yesh, and expressing the completed act by the perfect conjugation; Greek uses echo for possession and the perfect tense for the abiding result.
roots_lines: Hebrew perfect conjugation — the form denoting completed action; ordinarily rendered by the English hath plus a participle.
Hebrew yesh (H3426) — there is; with the preposition le it supplies the sense of having, since Hebrew lacks the verb.
Greek echo (G2192) — to have, to hold; the ordinary verb of possession.
Greek perfect tense — a past action with a standing present result; the tense of it is written and God hath cleansed.
Saxon hæfþ — the Old English third singular present, worn down in modern speech to has.
usage: Of a divine act already finished and therefore binding: What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common (Acts 10:15).
Of a purpose settled beyond reversal: For the LORD of hosts hath purposed, and who shall disannul it? (Isaiah 14:27).
Of sin completed in the heart before the hand moves: hath committed adultery with her already in his heart (Matthew 5:28).
scriptures: And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.
For the LORD of hosts hath purposed, and who shall disannul it? and his hand is stretched out, and who shall turn it back?
But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.
But of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of the garden, God hath said, Ye shall not eat of it, neither shall ye touch it, lest ye die.

pos: v. (second person singular present of have; rendering Hebrew perfect forms with second-person subject, Greek echeis)
etymology: From Saxon hæfst, the second person singular present of habban. It follows thou as hath follows he. Like hath it serves both for possession and as the auxiliary forming the perfect tense.
biblical_def: Hast is thou hast — what one person possesses, or what one person has done. It carries the first question God ever asked about guilt: “Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?” (Genesis 3:11). The question is not for God's information but for Adam's confession, and the perfect tense makes evasion useless, since the deed is done and standing. The same form carries the sweetest acknowledgements in the Psalms: “For thou hast girded me with strength to battle” (2 Samuel 22:40), “Thou hast delivered me from the strivings of the people” (Psalm 18:43). It also carries the psalmist's hardest complaints, spoken to God rather than about Him: “But thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed” (Psalm 89:38). And it appears in the mouth of the wicked servant returning his master's money unused: “lo, there thou hast that is thine” (Matthew 25:25). Praise, protest, and self-justification all use the same verb, and all three are addressed to a Person who already knows the answer.
webster_summary: The second person singular of the present tense of have; used only with thou. In Scripture it frames the first question of guilt in Eden, the psalmist's acknowledgements and complaints, and the excuse of the unprofitable servant.
webster_full: HAST, v. [Sax. hæfst.] The second person singular of the present tense of have; as, thou hast.
2. To possess; to hold; as, thou hast riches.
3. As an auxiliary, it forms the perfect tense; as, thou hast spoken, thou hast done.
4. It is used only with thou; with ye or you the form is have.
5. In Scripture, Hast thou eaten of the tree? Gen. 3; thou hast delivered me from the strivings of the people, Psa. 18.
corruption_summary: God's question in Eden is commonly read as though the Almighty were gathering information, which makes it either redundant or dishonest. It is neither: it is the summons to confession, and the whole biblical doctrine of repentance is contained in the form of it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is confession as God's appointed means of dealing with known sin. The LORD does not ask Hast thou eaten because He is uncertain; He is omniscient, and the fig leaves had already answered Him. He asks because a sinner must say it himself. The pattern holds throughout Scripture: Cain is asked where his brother is, David is confronted by Nathan, Peter is asked three times whether he loves the Lord. In every case the question invites the words that repentance requires.

Adam's reply is the first evasion in human history and remains the model of all the others — The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat. The confession is technically complete and morally worthless, because it arrives at the truth only after routing the blame through the wife and, past her, through God Himself. The parable of the talents shows the same instinct dressed as piety: I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, there thou hast that is thine. Both men answer the question. Neither one repents.
roots_summary: Hebrew expresses thou hast by the second person perfect of the verb, or by yesh with a preposition for possession; Greek uses echeis and the second singular perfect; Saxon hæfst gives the English form.
roots_lines: Hebrew second person perfect — the completed act with thou as subject; the form of the LORD's question in Genesis 3:11.
Hebrew 'akal (H398) — to eat; the verb in the first question of guilt put to man.
Greek echeis (G2192) — thou hast; the second person singular present of echo.
Greek perfect tense — a completed act with abiding result; underlies most of the Authorized Version's thou hast.
Saxon hæfst — the Old English second singular present, retained with thou in the Authorized Version.
usage: Of the first summons to confession: Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee? (Genesis 3:11).
Of deliverance acknowledged to God: Thou hast delivered me from the strivings of the people (Psalm 18:43).
Of the unprofitable servant returning what he never used: lo, there thou hast that is thine (Matthew 25:25).
scriptures: And he said, Who told thee that thou wast naked? Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?
Thou hast delivered me from the strivings of the people; and thou hast made me the head of the heathen: a people whom I have not known shall serve me.
But thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed.
And I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, there thou hast that is thine.

pos: v. (second person singular past of have; rendering Hebrew and Greek pluperfect and conditional constructions)
etymology: The past of hast, from Saxon hæfdest. In the Authorized Version it appears most often in conditions contrary to fact — if thou hadst — where something did not happen and the consequence therefore did not follow.
biblical_def: Hadst is thou hadst, and its characteristic use in Scripture is the unbearable conditional: the thing that would have been, had something else been. Martha meets Christ four days too late and says it plainly — “Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died” (John 11:21). The sentence is grief and faith together, and the Lord does not rebuke it. Over the city that would not receive Him He says, “If thou hadst known, even thou, at least in this thy day, the things which belong unto thy peace! but now they are hid from thine eyes” (Luke 19:42), and the sentence breaks off unfinished, as such sentences do. Isaiah puts the same construction in God's mouth as a lament over Israel's disobedience: “O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments! then had thy peace been as a river” (Isaiah 48:18). But the word also reaches back before all conditions to the eternity of God: “or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God” (Psalm 90:2). One tense holds both the might-have-been of the creature and the always-was of the Creator.
webster_summary: The second person singular of the past tense of have; used chiefly in conditions contrary to fact. In Scripture it carries Martha's grief, Christ's lament over Jerusalem, God's O that thou hadst hearkened, and the eternity that preceded the world.
webster_full: HADST, v. [Sax. hæfdest.] The second person singular of the past tense of have; as, thou hadst.
2. It is used in conditional and subjunctive clauses; as, if thou hadst been here.
3. As an auxiliary it forms the pluperfect tense; as, thou hadst spoken before he came.
4. It is used only with thou; with ye or you the form is had.
5. In Scripture, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died, John 11; O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments, Isa. 48.
corruption_summary: The lament O that thou hadst hearkened is regularly enlisted to prove that God's purposes can be defeated by human refusal. Scripture holds both together without embarrassment: God decrees the end, and God genuinely grieves over sin He has not decreed to prevent.
corruption_paragraphs: Open theism (Pinnock, Boyd, Sanders) reads the divine laments of Isaiah 48:18 and Luke 19:42 as evidence that God did not know and could not secure the outcome — that the future is open even to Him and His plans are genuinely frustrated. This departs from the classical attributes confessed by every historic creed and by the 1689: God is omniscient, immutable, and impassible, and He declares the end from the beginning. The lament is not ignorance discovering a disappointment. It is God expressing, in the only language creatures possess, His real hatred of the sin and His real compassion toward the sinner.

The opposite error is a hard fatalism that will not let such sentences be felt at all — that hurries past Christ's tears over Jerusalem to restate the decree. But it is the incarnate Son who weeps in Luke 19, and His grief is as real as His sovereignty. The Reformed tradition has never taught that the decree makes lament insincere; it teaches that God's revealed will genuinely commands what His secret will has not decreed to give, and that the sinner's ruin is therefore entirely his own fault. Both truths stand, and the man who drops either one has stopped reading the text in front of him.
roots_summary: Hebrew forms the contrary-to-fact condition with lu and the perfect; Greek uses ei with the aorist or pluperfect in the protasis and an in the apodosis; English marks it by hadst with the pluperfect.
roots_lines: Hebrew lu (H3863) — O that, if only; the particle of the wish or condition contrary to fact, as at Isaiah 48:18.
Greek ei with an — the second-class condition, contrary to fact; the construction of John 11:21.
Greek ginosko (G1097) — to know; the verb behind if thou hadst known in Luke 19:42.
Hebrew shama' (H8085) — to hear, to hearken, to obey; the verb of the divine lament in Isaiah 48:18.
Saxon hæfdest — the Old English past second singular of habban, to have.
usage: Of grief spoken directly to Christ: Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died (John 11:21).
Of Christ's lament over a city that would not know its day: If thou hadst known, even thou (Luke 19:42).
Of the eternity of God before creation: or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world (Psalm 90:2).
scriptures: Then said Martha unto Jesus, Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.
Saying, If thou hadst known, even thou, at least in this thy day, the things which belong unto thy peace! but now they are hid from thine eyes.
O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments! then had thy peace been as a river, and thy righteousness as the waves of the sea:
Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.

pos: v. (third person singular present of do; rendering Hebrew imperfect forms, Greek present indicative)
etymology: From Saxon deþ, the third person singular present of don, to do. It stands where modern English has does, and serves both as a full verb and as the auxiliary of emphasis and of the question.
biblical_def: Doth is the older does, and Scripture uses it in three characteristic ways. As an auxiliary of the question it appears in the serpent's insinuation and in the sneer of the wicked: “For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened” (Genesis 3:5), and “How doth God know? and is there knowledge in the most High?” (Psalm 73:11). Both attack the same attribute from opposite directions — the first says God knows too much and is therefore withholding, the second says He knows too little and is therefore safe to defy. As a plain present it marks steady, characteristic action: “The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her” (Proverbs 31:11), a trust that is not an event but a settled condition of the marriage. And it marks the quiet, continuous action of decay against which the Lord warns: treasure laid up in heaven is where “neither moth nor rust doth corrupt” (Matthew 6:20). The verb is unremarkable in itself, which is why it is worth noticing where it falls.
webster_summary: The third person singular of the present tense of do; the older form of does. In Scripture it frames the serpent's question about what God knows, the scoffer's denial that He knows, the husband's settled trust, and the slow work of moth and rust.
webster_full: DOTH, v. [Sax. deþ.] The third person singular of the present tense of do; contracted in modern usage to does.
2. To perform; to execute; to bring to pass; as, he doth all things well.
3. As an auxiliary it forms the emphatic and the interrogative; as, he doth know; doth God know?
4. It is retained in the solemn style and throughout the common version of the Scriptures.
5. In Scripture, For God doth know, Gen. 3; where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, Matt. 6.
corruption_summary: The two great assaults on God's knowledge are both framed as questions with this verb: the serpent's God doth know, which makes omniscience a motive for envy, and the scoffer's How doth God know?, which makes it a fiction. Both are answered by the same doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: The serpent's method in Genesis 3:5 is not to deny that God knows but to poison the fact. God doth know — and therefore, the insinuation runs, He is keeping something back; His prohibition is not protection but jealousy. This remains the most effective attack on God's character available, because it concedes His attributes and impugns His motives. Every temptation that presents obedience as deprivation is a repetition of it, and the answer is not a defence of God's knowledge but of His goodness: the same God who withheld one tree had freely given all the rest.

Psalm 73:11 attacks from the other side, and Asaph is honest that he nearly agreed. The prosperity of the wicked suggested to him that God either does not see or does not care, and the psalm records how close that reasoning came to overthrowing him. The turn comes when he goes into the sanctuary and understands their end. Practical atheism of this kind is more common in the church than theoretical atheism ever was: men who confess omniscience in the creed and live as though the account were never to be rendered. The doctrine of divine knowledge is not an abstraction but the ground of the fear of God.
roots_summary: Hebrew has no auxiliary answering to do; the emphatic and interrogative senses are carried by particles and word order. Greek uses the present indicative and the interrogative particles. Saxon deþ gives the English form.
roots_lines: Hebrew yada' (H3045) — to know; the verb in both the serpent's claim and Asaph's question.
Hebrew 'asah (H6213) — to do, to make, to accomplish; the ordinary verb of action rendered by do.
Greek aphanizo (G853) — to make to disappear, to corrupt or consume; the verb of moth and rust in Matthew 6:20.
Greek interrogative particles — Greek asks a question by particle and context rather than by an auxiliary such as doth.
Saxon deþ — the Old English third singular present of don, worn down to modern does.
usage: Of the serpent turning God's knowledge into a motive for suspicion: For God doth know (Genesis 3:5).
Of the scoffer denying that God knows at all: How doth God know? (Psalm 73:11).
Of the settled trust of a husband in a virtuous wife: The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her (Proverbs 31:11).
scriptures: For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.
And they say, How doth God know? and is there knowledge in the most High?
The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, so that he shall have no need of spoil.
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:

pos: v. (second person singular past of do; rendering Hebrew perfect forms, Greek aorist)
etymology: The past of dost, from Saxon dydest. It is used with thou alone, both as a full verb of past action and as the auxiliary that makes a past statement emphatic or interrogative.
biblical_def: Didst is thou didst — the past deed of one person, most often God's. The psalms use it to recite what God has actually done, which is the settled Hebrew method of praying: not describing His character in the abstract but reciting His acts. “Thou didst make me hope when I was upon my mother's breasts” (Psalm 22:9) traces faith itself back to God's work in infancy. “Thou, O God, didst send a plentiful rain, whereby thou didst confirm thine inheritance, when it was weary” (Psalm 68:9) sets providence and covenant in one sentence. Habakkuk's great prayer is built almost entirely of such verbs: “Thou didst march through the land in indignation, thou didst thresh the heathen in anger” (Habakkuk 3:12). The word is equally at home in rebuke, where it recalls a past failure to act: Pharaoh asks Abram, “why didst thou not tell me that she was thy wife?” (Genesis 12:18) — a pagan king reproving the friend of God for a half-truth, which is one of the more humbling sentences in Genesis.
webster_summary: The second person singular of the past tense of do; used only with thou. In Scripture it is the verb of recital — the psalmist and the prophet rehearsing before God the things God has actually done — and of reproof for what was left undone.
webster_full: DIDST, v. [Sax. dydest.] The second person singular of the past tense of do; as, thou didst.
2. To have performed, executed or brought to pass; as, thou didst well.
3. As an auxiliary it forms the emphatic and interrogative past; as, thou didst send; why didst thou go?
4. It is used only with thou; with ye or you the form is did.
5. In Scripture, thou didst make me hope, Psa. 22; Thou didst march through the land in indignation, Hab. 3.
corruption_summary: Prayer has largely stopped reciting what God has done and now mostly reports how the one praying feels. Scripture's prayers are built on past-tense verbs, and the loss of that habit leaves petition without ground and thanksgiving without content.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is the recital of God's acts as the substance of prayer. Habakkuk 3, Psalm 68, Psalm 105, Nehemiah 9, and Stephen's defence in Acts 7 are all built the same way: they rehearse history. This is not a rhetorical device. It is how faith reasons — the God who divided the sea is the God now being asked, and the petition rests on the precedent. A prayer with no past tense in it has nothing to stand on but the sincerity of the one praying.

The habit is worth restoring at the family table and in the closet as well as in the pulpit. Israel was commanded to teach children by rehearsing events, and the Passover liturgy exists to put the past tense in a child's mouth. Where prayer becomes purely present and personal, the next generation inherits sentiment rather than testimony. Psalm 22:9 shows how far back the recital can reach: thou didst make me hope when I was upon my mother's breasts — even the earliest stirrings of trust are God's work and are to be named as such.
roots_summary: Hebrew uses the perfect conjugation for completed past action, often with the pronoun written out for emphasis; Greek uses the aorist indicative; English marks the emphatic and interrogative past by the auxiliary didst.
roots_lines: Hebrew perfect with expressed pronoun — the emphatic thou didst, as in the recitals of Habakkuk 3.
Hebrew batach (H982) and yachal (H3176) — to trust and to hope; the verbs of Psalm 22:9.
Greek aorist indicative — the simple past of completed action, ordinarily rendered by the English past or by didst.
Hebrew tsa'ad (H6805) — to march or step; the verb of the LORD's advance in Habakkuk 3:12.
Saxon dydest — the Old English past second singular of don, to do.
usage: Of faith traced back to God's work in infancy: thou didst make me hope when I was upon my mother's breasts (Psalm 22:9).
Of providence confirming a weary inheritance: thou didst send a plentiful rain (Psalm 68:9).
Of a pagan king reproving a patriarch: why didst thou not tell me that she was thy wife? (Genesis 12:18).
scriptures: But thou art he that took me out of the womb: thou didst make me hope when I was upon my mother's breasts.
Thou, O God, didst send a plentiful rain, whereby thou didst confirm thine inheritance, when it was weary.
Thou didst march through the land in indignation, thou didst thresh the heathen in anger.
And Pharaoh called Abram, and said, What is this that thou hast done unto me? why didst thou not tell me that she was thy wife?

pos: v. (second person singular of shall; rendering Hebrew imperfect of command, Greek future indicative)
etymology: From Saxon scealt, second person singular of sceal, to owe or be obliged. The root sense is obligation, not mere futurity — a fact that governs its use in the law. Thou shalt is not a prediction about the future; it is a bond laid on the person addressed.
biblical_def: Shalt is the second person singular of shall, and it is the verb of the commandment. The Decalogue is built of it: “Thou shalt have no other gods before me”, “Thou shalt not kill”, and eight more, every one singular and every one binding a particular Israelite rather than the nation collectively. The old English sense of obligation is the reason the translators chose it, and it is why the commandments read as debts owed rather than events foreseen. But the same word also carries the warning — “in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die” — and the promise, as when Job is told, “the Almighty shall be thy defence, and thou shalt have plenty of silver” (Job 22:25). It governs the sabbath of the land: “thou shalt neither sow thy field, nor prune thy vineyard” (Leviticus 25:4), a command that required Israel to trust God's provision for a year at a time. Obligation, threat, and promise all run through this one form, which is fitting, since in Scripture they are never far apart.
webster_summary: The second person singular of shall; used only with thou. Its root sense is obligation rather than futurity, which is why it is the verb of the Decalogue — thou shalt and thou shalt not bind the person addressed rather than predicting what he will do.
webster_full: SHALT, v. [Sax. scealt.] The second person singular of shall; as, thou shalt.
2. The primary sense of shall is to owe, to be under obligation; hence its use in commands and laws.
3. In the second and third persons it expresses promise, command, determination or threatening.
4. It is used only with thou; with ye or you the form is shall.
5. In Scripture, Thou shalt have no other gods before me, Exo. 20; Thou shalt not kill, Exo. 20.
corruption_summary: The commandments are widely reduced to advice, ideals, or descriptions of a flourishing life — suggestions a man may weigh. The verb forbids that reading: shalt is the language of obligation imposed by a Lawgiver, and its force does not depend on the hearer's agreement.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors flatten the imperative. The first empties the law of authority by recasting it as wisdom for human flourishing — the commandments become sound advice, useful because they work, and therefore negotiable when they appear not to. The second empties it by antinomianism, treating the moral law as wholly abolished for the believer so that thou shalt not no longer addresses him at all. The 1689 Confession answers both: the moral law forever binds all, justified persons as well as others, though believers are not under it as a covenant of works for justification.

The right use of the imperative is the one the Reformed tradition has always taught. The law shows the sinner his guilt and drives him to Christ; it restrains evil in society; and it directs the believer's obedience out of gratitude, not for acceptance. Christ Himself intensified rather than relaxed it, moving each thou shalt not inward to the heart. To recover the weight of the word is not legalism, which is the attempt to be justified by keeping it; it is simply hearing the Lawgiver speak in the mood He actually used.
roots_summary: Hebrew commands by the imperative or by the imperfect with the negative lo', which is the absolute prohibition of the Decalogue; Greek renders these by the future indicative, which is why the New Testament citations read thou shalt not.
roots_lines: Hebrew lo' (H3808) — not; with the imperfect it forms the absolute, permanent prohibition of the Ten Commandments.
Hebrew imperfect of command — a form expressing binding obligation rather than simple future time.
Greek future indicative — the form used in the Septuagint and the New Testament to render the Hebrew prohibitions.
Saxon sceal — to owe, to be obliged; the root sense that made shall the proper verb for law.
Hebrew mitzvah (H4687) — a commandment; that which is laid upon a man by authority.
usage: Of the first commandment binding each Israelite singly: Thou shalt have no other gods before me (Exodus 20:3).
Of the sixth commandment in its briefest form: Thou shalt not kill (Exodus 20:13).
Of the sabbath required of the land itself: thou shalt neither sow thy field, nor prune thy vineyard (Leviticus 25:4).
scriptures: Thou shalt have no other gods before me.
But in the seventh year shall be a sabbath of rest unto the land, a sabbath for the LORD: thou shalt neither sow thy field, nor prune thy vineyard.
Yea, the Almighty shall be thy defence, and thou shalt have plenty of silver.

pos: v. (second person singular of will; rendering Hebrew imperfect of volition, Greek theleis and the future)
etymology: From Saxon wilt, second person singular of willan, to will or desire. Its root sense is volition, as the root sense of shall is obligation — a distinction the older grammarians guarded carefully and modern usage has lost. Distinguish it from the unrelated verb to wilt, to droop.
biblical_def: Wilt is the second person singular of will, and its proper force is desire or determination rather than bare futurity. Abram uses it to press God about the promise: “Lord GOD, what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless” (Genesis 15:2), and the answer is the covenant of the seed and the stars. The psalmists use it to hold God to His own character: “With the merciful thou wilt shew thyself merciful, and with the upright man thou wilt shew thyself upright” (2 Samuel 22:26); “For thou, LORD, wilt bless the righteous” (Psalm 5:12). They also use it to complain of delay without abandoning faith: “O LORD God of hosts, how long wilt thou be angry against the prayer of thy people?” (Psalm 80:4). In the Gospels the word most often falls from Christ's lips as a question that requires the hearer to state what he actually wants — the servants asking whether they shall gather the tares, the blind man asked what he would have done, the impotent man at the pool asked whether he wills to be made whole. Scripture takes the human will seriously enough to interrogate it.
webster_summary: The second person singular of will; used only with thou. Its root sense is volition and determination, as distinguished from the obligation carried by shalt. In Scripture it frames Abram's question about the promise, the psalmist's appeal to God's character, and Christ's questions to those who came to Him.
webster_full: WILT, v. [Sax. wilt.] The second person singular of will; as, thou wilt.
2. The primary sense of will is to desire, to be inclined, to determine; hence its use in promise and resolution.
3. In the first person it expresses determination; in the second and third, prediction or permission.
4. WILT, v.i. To begin to wither; to lose freshness. This is a wholly distinct word.
5. In Scripture, what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless? Gen. 15; how long wilt thou be angry? Psa. 80.
corruption_summary: The will of man is the point where two errors meet: a libertarian free will that makes the sinner the deciding cause of his own salvation, and a fatalism that treats his willing as unreal. Scripture's questions — wilt thou be made whole? — presuppose a will that genuinely chooses and is genuinely bound.
corruption_paragraphs: The Reformed doctrine is not that man has no will but that his will is not free toward God until it is freed. The 1689 Confession states it exactly: man by his fall into a state of sin has wholly lost all ability of will to any spiritual good accompanying salvation, and is not able by his own strength to convert himself; when God converts a sinner He frees him from his natural bondage and enables him freely to will and to do that which is spiritually good. The sinner therefore always does what he wills, and what he wills is sin, until grace renews the willing itself. Arminian theology grants the fallen will a decisive vote it does not possess; the result is a salvation that finally depends on the creature.

The pastoral consequence is not passivity but the opposite. Because the will is real, Christ questions it: Wilt thou be made whole? He asks a man who had lain thirty-eight years by the pool. Because the will is bound, the answer must be given by grace. Preachers therefore command what only God can grant, and they are right to do so, since the command is the very instrument the Spirit uses. Whosoever will may come; and that any man wills to come is itself the evidence of a work already begun in him.
roots_summary: Hebrew expresses volition by the imperfect, sometimes strengthened by 'abah (to be willing) or chaphets (to delight in); Greek uses thelo and boulomai for willing and the future indicative for simple futurity.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'abah (H14) — to be willing, to consent; almost always used in the negative of Israel's refusal.
Hebrew chaphets (H2654) — to delight in, to take pleasure in; the willing that arises from desire rather than duty.
Greek thelo (G2309) — to will, to wish, to desire; the verb in Christ's questions to those who sought Him.
Greek boulomai (G1014) — to purpose, to determine; willing considered as settled counsel.
Saxon willan — to will or desire; the root that distinguishes will from shall, which means to owe.
usage: Of pressing God about an unfulfilled promise: what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless? (Genesis 15:2).
Of appealing to God's consistency with His own character: With the merciful thou wilt shew thyself merciful (2 Samuel 22:26).
Of complaint at delay that does not abandon faith: how long wilt thou be angry against the prayer of thy people? (Psalm 80:4).
scriptures: And Abram said, Lord GOD, what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless, and the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus?
With the merciful thou wilt shew thyself merciful, and with the upright man thou wilt shew thyself upright.
O LORD God of hosts, how long wilt thou be angry against the prayer of thy people?
For thou, LORD, wilt bless the righteous; with favour wilt thou compass him as with a shield.
